payload.throughline: Read the functional group, identify the reactive atom and leaving group, then use oxidation level, substitution pathway, acyl addition–elimination, and boundary conditions to predict the product.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: locate the electrophilic carbon in a familiar carbonyl and the nucleophilic atom in an alcohol. This activates prerequisite relations V3-EDG-145568 and V3-EDG-407357; uncertainty routes to the exact noncredit handoff V3-LES-560768.

Goal: predict alcohol acidity and hydrogen bonding, oxidation, and SN1/SN2 substitution. The hard-prerequisite handoff preserves V3-LES-560768 and KCs V3-KC-669728, V3-KC-338522, V3-KC-460552, V3-KC-040072, and V3-KC-060298 rather than reteaching its carbonyl and enolate scope here.

An alcohol oxygen can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, usually raising boiling point relative to a similar nonpolar molecule. Small alcohols mix with water more readily than long-chain alcohols because the hydrocarbon portion increasingly opposes solvation.
Alcohols are weak acids; deprotonation forms an alkoxide. Factors that stabilize negative charge favor acidity.

A primary alcohol can oxidize to an aldehyde and, under stronger conditions, a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol oxidizes to a ketone. A tertiary alcohol lacks the needed hydrogen on the carbinol carbon for ordinary oxidation without carbon–carbon bond cleavage.
The hydroxyl group is a poor leaving group unless activated. Primary centers generally favor SN2 with a strong nucleophile; tertiary centers can favor SN1 under ionizing conditions.
Mental model: oxygen controls intermolecular forces and acidity; the carbon bearing oxygen controls oxidation class and substitution pathway.

Think aloud: I classify the carbon bearing OH before choosing chemistry. A secondary carbon gives a ketone on oxidation. For substitution, a primary activated center is accessible to backside attack, while a tertiary center is too hindered for ordinary SN2.
Worked example: 2-propanol has a secondary carbinol carbon, so oxidation gives acetone, a ketone.
A primary alkyl sulfonate ester reacting with a strong nucleophile follows SN2 and inverts configuration if that carbon is stereogenic.
Guided practice: mark the carbinol carbon as primary, secondary, or tertiary before selecting oxidation or substitution.
Less support: use one structural cue to predict hydrogen bonding or oxidation product class.
On your own: choose the dominant behavior for a fresh alcohol and condition set.

Boundary: a tertiary alcohol is not “more oxidized” merely because its carbon has more carbon substituents. Also, neutral OH is not an effective leaving group in ordinary substitution until it is activated.
Near exit: select oxidation and substitution behavior from a familiar alcohol structure.
Changed-task exit: use a molecule with two nonequivalent alcohol sites to predict site-selective oxidation.
Repair the classification function: count carbon groups attached to the carbinol carbon, then ask whether it carries the hydrogen needed for ordinary oxidation.
Fresh near re-entry: classify a different alcohol and predict its product class.
Repair the site-selection function: analyze each OH-bearing carbon independently; a primary site can oxidize while a tertiary site remains unchanged under ordinary selective conditions.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: choose the reacting site in a new diol without reusing the prior skeleton.
Recap: hydrogen bonding comes from oxygen; oxidation follows alcohol class; substitution requires an activated leaving group and a pathway compatible with steric substitution.
Starting check: decide whether a step masks OH or improves its leaving-group ability. A prerequisite miss uses either exact edge to V3-LES-560768 before target work.

Goal: predict why an alcohol is protected and what mesylate or tosylate preparation accomplishes. The exact prerequisite handoff preserves prior carbonyl addition and enolate reasoning rather than embedding it as assumed hidden knowledge.
Protection converts an alcohol into a less reactive derivative so another functional group can undergo a planned step. Deprotection later restores the OH.

Mesylate and tosylate formation converts ROH into a sulfonate ester, ROMs or ROTs. Activation occurs at oxygen and creates a good leaving group without replacing the carbon–oxygen bond at that moment.
A later nucleophile can displace the sulfonate at carbon. If that displacement is SN2 at a stereocenter, the carbon configuration inverts; activation alone does not cause that inversion.
Mental model: a protecting group is a removable cover; a sulfonate is a removable handle. Covering prevents reaction, while activation prepares a later reaction.

Think aloud: if a synthesis needs to oxidize an aldehyde-sensitive partner while retaining an alcohol, I protect the alcohol. If the goal is to replace OH with a nucleophile, I activate it as a sulfonate, then analyze the separate substitution step.
Worked example: protect ROH, perform a reaction elsewhere, then deprotect to recover ROH. The OH returns at the same carbon.
Converting a chiral alcohol to ROTs changes the oxygen substituent but not the stereocenter. A later SN2 displacement inverts that carbon.
Guided practice: label each step MASK, UNMASK, ACTIVATE, or DISPLACE before predicting the product.
Less support: identify whether OH is preserved for later or prepared to leave.
On your own: select the required sequence for a new synthetic constraint.

Boundary: tosylation is not itself nucleophilic substitution at carbon. Protection is also not activation: a protected alcohol is intentionally less reactive, whereas a sulfonate ester is prepared to leave.
Near exit: choose protection or activation for a familiar synthetic goal.
Changed-task exit: track stereochemistry through oxygen activation followed by carbon-centered SN2 displacement.
Repair the purpose function: ask whether the synthesis wants OH silent or wants OH replaced. Silent means protect; replacement means activate.
Fresh near re-entry: choose a step for a different synthetic conflict.
Repair the stereochemical trace: activation changes the oxygen substituent and retains carbon configuration; the later SN2 step attacks carbon and inverts it.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: trace a new chiral alcohol through mesylation and a different nucleophile.
Recap: protect to preserve OH through another reaction; deprotect to restore it; form mesylate or tosylate to create a leaving group for a later substitution.
Starting check: identify the carboxyl carbon and its adjacent 2-position. Prerequisite uncertainty follows the exact carbonyl/enolate handoff.
Goal: predict carboxylic-acid derivative formation, reduction, decarboxylation, and 2-position substitution without extending beyond the listed transformation families.
Carboxylic acids can form esters with alcohol-derived nucleophiles and amides with nitrogen nucleophiles after suitable activation or condensation conditions.
Reduction lowers the carboxyl carbon oxidation state, commonly producing a primary alcohol under strong reduction conditions.

Decarboxylation removes the carboxyl carbon as carbon dioxide from a suitably activated framework. The 2-position, also called the alpha carbon, is directly adjacent to the carboxyl carbon and can undergo substitution when activated.
Mental model: at the carbonyl carbon, swap the OH-derived group for a derivative or reduce the carbon; at the adjacent carbon, substitute; in decarboxylation, remove the carboxyl carbon.

Think aloud: I first mark carbon 1 as the carboxyl carbon and carbon 2 as adjacent. Alcohol plus acid points to ester formation; loss of CO2 lowers carbon count by one; substitution at carbon 2 leaves the carboxyl carbon in place.
Worked example: ethanoic acid plus methanol under ester-forming conditions gives methyl ethanoate and water.
A three-carbon acid that decarboxylates loses its carboxyl carbon, so the retained carbon skeleton has two carbons.
Guided practice: mark whether the transformation changes the acyl substituent, oxidation state, carbon count, or 2-position group.
Less support: infer product class from one reagent role and one carbon-map cue.
On your own: distinguish derivative formation, reduction, and decarboxylation.
Boundary: ester formation does not reduce the carbonyl carbon. Two-position substitution also does not replace the carbonyl OH; it changes the adjacent carbon.
Near exit: classify the product family of a familiar carboxylic-acid transformation.
Changed-task exit: use carbon-count evidence and gas release to identify decarboxylation.

Repair the transformation function: track carbon count and the atom attached to the acyl carbon. Same count with OR or NR attachment indicates derivative formation; lower oxidation state indicates reduction.
Fresh near re-entry: classify a different acid transformation with a new nucleophile.
Repair the carbon-map function: number the carboxyl carbon as 1. CO2 loss removes carbon 1; 2-position substitution changes the adjacent carbon but retains carbon 1.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: distinguish alpha substitution from decarboxylation using a new carbon count.
Recap: form derivatives at the acyl carbon, reduce its oxidation state, lose it during decarboxylation, or substitute at the adjacent 2-position.
Starting check: distinguish carbonyl addition from addition followed by elimination. A missing carbonyl prerequisite routes through the exact V3-LES-560768 handoff.
Goal: predict acid-derivative substitution, transesterification, and amide hydrolysis by following the shared addition–elimination mechanism.
A nucleophile attacks the acyl carbon, the carbonyl π bond opens onto oxygen, and a tetrahedral intermediate forms.
The intermediate collapses: the carbonyl reforms and a leaving group departs. The net result is substitution at the acyl carbon.

In transesterification, one ester alkoxy group is exchanged for another alcohol-derived group. In amide hydrolysis, the acyl–nitrogen bond is replaced by an oxygen-containing group, yielding a carboxylic acid or carboxylate and a nitrogen-containing product depending on conditions.
Mental model: add to make a tetrahedron, then eliminate to restore the carbonyl. Keep the incoming group and identify the departing group.
Think aloud: methoxide attacks an ester carbonyl. I draw the tetrahedral intermediate, then collapse it to expel the original alkoxy group. The new ester carries the incoming methoxy group.
Worked example: ethyl acetate plus methanol under exchange conditions forms methyl acetate plus ethanol at equilibrium. The acyl carbon remains; the alkoxy group changes.
Hydrolysis of an amide replaces the nitrogen substituent at the acyl carbon with an oxygen-containing group.
Guided practice: label IN, OUT, and STAYS on each acyl substitution scheme.
Less support: identify the product derivative from the incoming nucleophile.
On your own: select a transesterification or hydrolysis product.
Boundary: nucleophilic addition to an aldehyde or ketone lacks an acyl leaving group and need not restore the carbonyl. Acyl substitution requires the elimination half of the mechanism.
Near exit: order the common acyl substitution mechanism and choose the product.
Changed-task exit: infer which ester alkoxy group is exchanged from a labeled alcohol reagent.
Repair the mechanism function: after attack, verify a tetrahedral carbon; during collapse, reform C=O before assigning the leaving group.
Fresh near re-entry: predict a new acid-derivative substitution with a different nucleophile.
Repair the group-tracking function: the incoming alcohol supplies the new ester OR group; the original OR group leaves as its alcohol after proton transfers.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: track a different labeled alkoxy group through exchange.

Recap: nucleophile adds, a tetrahedral intermediate forms, the carbonyl reforms, and a leaving group exits; transesterification swaps OR groups and amide hydrolysis replaces nitrogen at the acyl carbon.
Starting check: compare ester and amide resonance donation. The exact prerequisite edges remain available for missing carbonyl classification.
Goal: compare acid-derivative reactivity using relative leaving-group ability, steric and electronic effects, and strain such as β-lactams.

A useful introductory order among the listed common derivatives is anhydride more reactive than ester, and ester more reactive than amide. Better leaving groups and a more electrophilic acyl carbon favor substitution.
Amide nitrogen donates strongly by resonance, reducing carbonyl electrophilicity; its leaving group is also strongly basic, so ordinary amides are relatively unreactive.

Electron withdrawal can increase carbonyl electrophilicity, steric crowding can hinder attack, and β-lactam ring strain twists the amide away from ideal resonance overlap, increasing reactivity relative to an unstrained amide.
Mental model: reaction needs entry and exit—nucleophile access to an electrophilic carbonyl and a group able to leave. Resonance, crowding, and strain tune those gates.

Think aloud: between an ester and amide, the amide has stronger nitrogen resonance donation and a poorer leaving group, so I rank the ester as more reactive. A β-lactam is an exception within amides because ring strain weakens resonance stabilization.
Worked example: an anhydride has a carboxylate-like leaving group and reacts more readily than an ester with an alkoxide leaving group.
An unstrained amide is resonance-stabilized, while a strained β-lactam cannot maintain the same planar overlap and is more susceptible to nucleophilic acyl attack.
Guided practice: compare leaving groups first, then resonance donation, steric access, and strain.
Less support: use one electronic or steric change to predict a relative-rate direction.
On your own: rank a fresh pair of derivatives.

Boundary: resonance stabilization is not the same as “no reaction.” It lowers relative reactivity. Steric and electronic factors can modify a ranking, and β-lactam strain can make a cyclic amide unusually reactive.
Near exit: rank anhydride, ester, and amide reactivity under comparable conditions.
Changed-task exit: explain why a β-lactam reacts faster than an unstrained amide despite sharing the amide functional group.
Repair the ranking function: identify the departing group and how strongly the attached heteroatom donates into the carbonyl. Better leaving plus weaker donation means greater reactivity.
Fresh near re-entry: compare a different derivative pair with new substituents.
Repair the strain function: a planar amide maximizes n-to-π* donation; a constrained β-lactam twists this geometry, weakens resonance, and leaves a more electrophilic carbonyl.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: use new structural evidence to compare a strained and unstrained amide.
Recap: leaving-group ability, resonance donation, steric access, electron withdrawal, and strain together control acid-derivative reactivity.
